# High-Performance LLM Inference: A Technical Deep Dive into Continuous Batching, KV Caches, and Advanced Decoding Strategies

The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in production environments presents a unique set of engineering challenges that differ significantly from traditional machine learning inference. Unlike computer vision or tabular data models, where inference is often a single, stateless forward pass, LLM inference is an autoregressive, stateful process. The generation of a single token depends on all previous tokens, creating a sequential dependency that fundamentally limits parallelism. To serve thousands of concurrent users with low latency and high throughput, modern inference servers have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to manage memory, schedule requests, and optimize computation. This tutorial explores the core pillars of high-performance LLM serving: the Key-Value (KV) Cache, Continuous Batching, Prefix Reuse, and Speculative Decoding, while analyzing the critical trade-offs between latency and throughput.

## 1. The Foundation: The Key-Value (KV) Cache

To understand modern inference optimization, one must first understand the computational bottleneck of the Transformer architecture. In a standard Transformer decoder, the self-attention mechanism computes attention scores between the current token and all previous tokens in the sequence. Mathematically, for a query vector $Q$ and key vectors $K$, the attention output is calculated as:

$$ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V $$

However, during the decode phase (generating new tokens one by one), the model generates one token at a time.
